newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate set to debate chemical weapons treaty.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate set to debate chemical weapons treaty.

text.p: The Senate begins debate on Wednesday on an international treaty outlawing chemical weapons, 82 years after choking clouds of poison gas first enveloped allied troops in the First World War.
The 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention, the first major post-Cold War arms control treaty and the first to ban a whole class of weapons, has been ratified by more than 70 countries.
Now the Senate, in votes on Thursday, will decide whether the United States will take part in the treaty that two Republican administrations helped negotiate and which goes into effect on April 29.
On April 22, 1915, German forces seeking to break a military stalemate, used chlorine gas in an attack against French and Canadian troops on the Western Front near Ypres.
Both sides used gas later in that war but it was not used in the Second World War, although new and more deadly gases had been developed.

Amid revulsion against such warfare and development of more effective weapons for battlefield use, the United States is committed to destroying its own gas stocks. The aim of the treaty, supporters say, is to get all other countries do so.
President Bill Clinton and an array of top administration officials have been lobbying hard for the treaty and Clinton said on Tuesday he was "quite optimistic" of Senate approval.
He picked up an ally among a key group of conservatiuve Republicans on Tuesday when Sen Alfonse D'Aamto of New York announced his support for the treaty.
But critics argue the treaty will lead to U.S. complacency about the chemical weapons threat while doing nothing to constrain countries posing such a threat, such as Iraq and Libya.

They also charge that inspection provisions would impose a burden on U.S. chemical companies, that the treaty cannot be verified and that the United States would be required to impart industrial secrets and sensitive information on chemical weapons countermeasures to potential adversaries.

Supporters say the burden on most firms would be slight and note that the Chemical Manufacturers Association, the main industry group, strongly backs the treaty. They defend the verification provisions while acknowledging that no verification can be perfect, and deny that the treaty would require the United States to hand over secrets.

The argument has pitted Clinton and his Democratic allies in the Senate against conservatives as both sides seek to win over uncommitted Republicans whose votes are needed to provide the two-thirds Senate majority needed for approval of treaties.

Torturous negotiations between the leading Senate foe of the treaty, Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms of North Carolina and his committee's top Democrat, Sen Joseph Biden of Delaware have produced agreement on 28 amendments to the Senate resolution consenting to the treaty's ratification.

But five other amendments remain in dispute and treaty supporters will try to eliminate them in a series of votes on Thursday. Four of the amendments are being described as "killers" that would bar U.S. participation in the treaty.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott, whose support is seen as a key to treaty approval, has said he is concerned about a treaty provision he says would require U.S. sharing of chemical technology with "rogue" nations -- a charge denied by treaty supporters.
"That is the critical point for me," Lott said over the weekend. "If we could work that out, we'll take a look at the whole thing."
One of the disputed amendments would require renegotiation to eliminate this provision from the treaty before the United States could ratify it.

Other "killer" amendments would set high verification standards and require the United States to withhold ratification until Russia and countries said to be sponsors of international terrorism sign on to the convention.
